source.title: HoneyBee: Progressive Instruction Finetuning of Large Language Models for Materials Science
source.authors: Yu Song; Santiago Miret; Huan Zhang; Bang Liu

record.tranche_reason: The study compares downstream task performance by model size in the new setting of materials-science instruction-finetuned models, but does not fit or measure pretraining scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The study reports downstream MatSci-NLP performance comparisons across model sizes. It does not measure held-out pretraining cross-entropy, fit scaling curves, test extrapolation, or allocate a fixed compute budget. Reported model sizes and task results cited from other work are not treated as findings of this study.
record.test_reason: This is a method paper on domain instruction finetuning (HoneyBee). Its only scale results compare two sizes, 7b and 13b, within each model family. Those comparisons are confounded with finetuning stage and family. They cannot show that downstream performance improves predictably with scale (V6). No loss curves, fits, extrapolation, compute allocation or shape study appear. Chinchilla is cited only in related work. The record's 'tests/T3' is overstated.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, but it misses the paper's main conclusion. The authors conclude that MatSci-Instruct's verified, progressively refined instruction data makes HoneyBee outperform LLaMA, Alpaca and materials-science BERT models, and that each stage improves it. They mention in passing that size matters for zero-shot performance in instruction-finetuned models (13b > 7b), while LLaMA-7b beats LLaMA-13b. They draw no scaling-law conclusions.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates instruction-finetuned models on downstream materials-science tasks rather than fitting loss-versus-size, data, or compute curves.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported size trend differs by model family: HoneyBee and Alpaca favor 13b, while LLaMA generally favors 7b.

fits_no_version.finding: Two-size downstream comparisons with mixed direction. 13b beats 7b for HoneyBee and Alpaca on zero-shot MatSci-NLP (Table 3) and for all families on GPT-4-judged instruction data (Table 2). Base LLaMA-7b beats LLaMA-13b on zero-shot MatSci-NLP.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Pairwise model-size comparisons on domain downstream tasks (direction of the size effect), not predictability of scaling.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP), 2023
record.problems: The size comparison covers only the reported model sizes and task setting; no uncertainty estimates or scaling-law fits are provided.
record.rows_left_out: No additional results bearing on tested claim versions were left out. Other scores in Tables 2 and 3 concern finetuning stages, instruction-data evaluation, or task comparisons rather than the scale trend summarized in these rows.

untested.parts: No shape comparison at fixed parameter count.
No power-law fit for finetuning, only two sizes.
No scaling curve or loss-to-task mapping; only 7b vs 13b comparisons.

record.verdict_notes: Table 3 text extraction is scrambled, so per-model values for the LLaMA and Alpaca rows are uncertain. The size effect is confounded with finetuning (LoRA, stage) and model family. The record's V6 supports/challenges labels are removed because two-point comparisons cannot test predictability.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute; power-law form and orders of magnitude.
No small-run fits or predictions for larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or compute-optimal parameter/token trends.
No controlled comparisons of depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
The study fine-tunes language models for materials science but does not test whether power-law scaling holds in fine-tuning or other training regimes.
Does not test a quantitative prediction from pretraining loss or a fitted scaling curve; comparisons are limited to the reported model sizes and MatSci-NLP setting.
No comparison of fitting choices, exponents, or curve bending.

rows.subject: HoneyBee-13b
rows.operation_detail: Compared zero-shot MatSci-NLP performance by parameter size.
rows.value: The text states that 13b parameter models outperform 7b for HoneyBee.
rows.note: The comparison is reported as a general statement; no specific aggregate score for this size comparison is given in the text.
rows.check: A two-point 7b vs 13b comparison of finetuned HoneyBee cannot show predictable scaling. The note saying no score is given is wrong: Table 3 zero-shot overall is HB-7b-Stage3 0.409/0.271 vs HB-13b-Stage3 0.557/0.417 (macro/micro F1).

rows.subject: Alpaca-13b
rows.operation_detail: Compared zero-shot MatSci-NLP performance by parameter size.
rows.value: The text states that 13b parameter models outperform 7b for Alpaca.
rows.note: The comparison is reported as a general statement; no specific aggregate score for this size comparison is given in the text.
rows.check: A two-point comparison that cannot bear on predictability. Table 3 does give numbers: Alpaca overall reads about 0.141/0.101 (7b) vs 0.202/0.145 (13b), though the table text is scrambled.

rows.subject: LLaMA-7b
rows.operation_detail: Compared zero-shot MatSci-NLP performance by parameter size.
rows.measure: MatSci-NLP task performance across tasks and overall score
rows.value: The text states that LLaMA-7b generally outperforms LLaMA-13b across most tasks and in the overall score.
rows.note: This is the study's explicit summary of the size comparison.
rows.check: A two-point comparison. The 7b > 13b result for base LLaMA on zero-shot MatSci-NLP comes with near-floor scores (about 0.1–0.2 F1), so it is weak evidence on scaling. It also conflicts with Table 2 (GPT-4-judged), where Llama-13b beats 7b (84.22 vs 78.81 accuracy).

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
